description: Typing props and useState — where TypeScript pays off in React.

screens.body:
React components pass data through props — and props are the #1 source of "undefined" bugs. You rename a prop in the parent, forget the child, and the app silently renders nothing.

TypeScript fixes this at the source: type your props, and renaming a prop becomes a compiler error in every component that uses it. The bug is impossible to ship.

options: Prop mistakes become compiler errors, not silent bugs
check.question: What do typed props give you?

screens.heading: Why typed React
screens.keyPoint: Typed props turn silent UI bugs into compiler errors.

screens.body:
Props are just an object, so you type them with an interface. Destructure the props in the parameter list and annotate with the interface.

Convention: name it Props, or ComponentNameProps for clarity in big files. Either way, every prop's type is now documented and checked.

check.question: How do you type destructured props?

screens.heading: Typing props with an interface
screens.keyPoint: interface Props + ({ name }: Props) — checked at every use.

screens.body:
Not every prop is required — mark optional ones with ?, and give defaults by destructuring with =.

Note the order: the ? goes on the interface property, the default goes in the destructuring. Together they mean "callers can skip it, and here's what we use instead."

options: size?: string in the interface, = "md" in destructuring
check.question: An optional size prop defaulting to "md":

screens.heading: Optional props and defaults
screens.keyPoint: ? in the interface, = default in destructuring.

screens.body:
useState takes a generic: useState<string>("…") means "this state holds a string." TypeScript then checks every setState call.

The common gotcha is state that starts empty: useState<User>(null) errors because null isn't a User. The fix is a union: useState<User | null>(null) — "a User, or nothing yet."

check.question: State holding a string, typed explicitly:

screens.heading: Typing useState
screens.keyPoint: useState<Type>(initial) — and User | null for "empty at first".

screens.body:
Event handlers get typed events. An input's onChange receives a ChangeEvent from an HTMLInputElement — and TypeScript knows e.target.value is a string.

You rarely memorize these; your editor autocompletes them. The skill is recognizing the pattern: React.SomethingEvent<HTMLElementType>.
screens.heading: Typing events

screens.body:
Components that wrap other components accept children — typed as React.ReactNode, which means "anything renderable": text, elements, arrays of them.

This is how layout components (Card, Modal, Page) stay flexible: they don't care what's inside, only where it goes.

check.question: The prop type for wrapped content:

screens.heading: The children prop

screens.body:
Put it together: typed props, typed state, typed event — a small component with zero places for a type bug to hide.

Read it top to bottom: the Props interface is the contract, useState<string> guards the state, the ChangeEvent types the handler. Every line is checked before the browser ever sees it.

screens.heading: Putting it together
screens.keyPoint: Props + state + events typed = no hiding spots for bugs.
